The algebraical integrals <math>\int\text{R}(x,y)dx</math> associated with this may as before be divided into those of the ''first kind'', which have no infinities, those of the ''second kind'', possessing only algebraical infinities, and those of the ''third kind'', for which logarithmic infinities enter. Here there is a certain number, <math>p</math>, greater than unity, of linearly independent integrals of the first kind; and this number <math>p</math> is unaltered by any birational transformation of the fundamental equation <math>f(x,y) = 0</math>; a rational function can be constructed with poles of the first order at <math>p+1</math> arbitrary positions <math>(x,y)</math>, satisfying <math>f(x,y) = 0</math>, but not with a fewer number unless their positions are chosen properly, a property we found for the case <math>p = 1</math>; and <math>p</math> is the number of linearly independent curves of order <math>n-3</math> passing through the double points of the curve of order <math>n</math> expressed by <math>f(x,y) = 0</math>. Again any integral of the second kind can be expressed as a sum of <math>p</math> integrals of this kind, with poles of the first order at arbitrary positions, together with rational functions and integrals of the first kind; and an integral of the second kind can be found with one pole of the first order of arbitrary position, and an integral of the third kind with two logarithmic infinities, also of arbitrary position; the corresponding properties for <math>p = 1</math> are proved above.

There is, however, a difference of essential kind in regard to the inversion of integrals of the first kind; if <math>u = \int\text{R}(x,y)dx</math> be such an integral, it can be shown, in common with all algebraic integrals associated with <math>f(x,y) = 0</math>, to have <math>2p</math> linearly independent additive constants of indeterminateness; the upper limit of the integral cannot therefore, as we have shown, be a single valued function of the value of the integral. The corresponding theorem, if <math>\int\text{R}_i(x,y)dx</math> denote one of the integrals of the first kind, is that the <math>p</math> equations

{{block center|<math>\int\text{R}_i(x_1,y_1)dx_1 + \dots + \int\text{R}_i(x_p,y_p)dx_p = u_i,</math>}}

{{block center|<math>\text{ZY}^2=a\text{X}^3+b\text{X}^2\text{Z}+c\text{XZ}^2+d\text{Z}^3</math>;}}

{{block center|<math>\text{ZY}^2=4\text{X}^3-g_2\text{XZ}^2-g_3\text{Z}^3</math>,}}

{{block center|<math>u=\int_{(\infty)}^{(x)}\frac{\text{Z}d\text{X}-\text{X}d\text{Z}}{\text{ZY}}</math>,}} where <math>(\infty)</math> denotes the point of inflection.

In virtue of the birational transformation this theorem can be deduced from the theorem that if any straight line cut the cubic <math>y^2=4x^3-g_2x-g_3</math>, in points <math>(u_1)</math>, <math>(u_2)</math>, <math>(u_3)</math>, the sum <math>u_1+u_2+u_3</math> is zero, or a period; or the general theorem is a corollary from Abel's theorem proved under § 17, ''Integrals of Algebraic Functions''. {{block center|<math>\text{F}(x)=4x^3-g_2x-g_3-(mx+n)^2=0</math>,}}
and is thus given by
{{block center|<math>\frac{dx}{y}=2\frac{x\delta m+\delta n}{\text{F}'(x)}</math>,}}
and the sum of three such fractions as that on the right for the three roots of <math>\text{F}(x)=0</math> is zero; hence <math>u_1+u_2+u_3</math> is independent of the straight line considered; if in particular this become the inflexional tangent each of <math>u_1</math>, <math>u_2</math>, <math>u_3</math> vanishes.
